questions.q: Why does a fully-meshed network, where every team's VNet or VPC peers directly with every other one, stop working at enterprise scale?
options: Peering connections automatically expire after 90 days on both Azure and AWS
Full mesh requires a dedicated ExpressRoute circuit for every pair of networks
The connection count grows roughly as N² against the number of networks, making review and firewall policy unmanageable
Azure and AWS both cap total VNets/VPCs per subscription or account at 10
questions.explain: A full mesh's connection count grows quadratically with the number of networks — tolerable at 5 teams, unmanageable at 50 — which is exactly the problem hub-and-spoke is designed to solve.

questions.q: What is the one fact about Azure VNet peering that makes the hub-and-spoke pattern work?
options: VNet peering is explicitly non-transitive — a spoke peered to the hub cannot automatically reach another spoke through it
VNet peering automatically routes all spoke-to-spoke traffic through Azure Firewall with no configuration needed
VNet peering only works within a single resource group
VNet peering requires both VNets to share the exact same address space
questions.explain: VNet peering's non-transitivity means a spoke peered to the hub cannot reach another peered spoke automatically — that forces the hub to be the only path, which an architect then controls with UDRs.

questions.q: On Azure, what mechanism actually forces a spoke's outbound traffic through the hub's firewall instead of straight to the internet?
options: A Network Security Group attached to the hub VNet only
A user-defined route (UDR) on the spoke subnet setting the 0.0.0.0/0 route's next hop to the hub's firewall/NVA
Azure Virtual WAN, which is required before any peering can be created
A DNS CNAME record pointing the spoke's traffic at the hub
questions.explain: A UDR on the spoke subnet overriding the default route (0.0.0.0/0) to point at the hub firewall or NVA's IP is what turns non-transitive peering into enforced centralized egress.

questions.q: How does AWS Transit Gateway differ from the classic Azure hub-and-spoke pattern built on VNet peering and UDRs?
options: Transit Gateway cannot connect to a VPN or Direct Connect link, only VPCs
Transit Gateway is a managed, natively transitive router that VPCs attach to, using route table associations instead of manually maintained UDRs per spoke
Transit Gateway requires every attached VPC to use identical CIDR ranges
Transit Gateway only supports a single VPC attachment per AWS account
questions.explain: Transit Gateway handles transitive routing natively through route table associations on attachments, rather than requiring an architect to hand-wire UDRs on every spoke the way classic Azure hub-and-spoke does.

questions.q: When does Azure Virtual WAN typically become the better choice over a hand-built hub VNet with manual UDRs?
options: Virtual WAN is never recommended and Microsoft advises against using it in production
Virtual WAN is only usable with a single spoke, so it never applies to multi-team designs
Virtual WAN should be used in place of Azure Firewall entirely and removes the need for any firewall
Once the number of spokes or regions makes manually keeping UDRs consistent across every spoke too error-prone to maintain by hand
questions.explain: Virtual WAN is Microsoft's managed hub, the closer Azure analog to Transit Gateway, and becomes the better option once hand-maintaining UDRs across many spokes/regions stops being manageable.
